answer: The recommendation in question was Martin Doerr's/ICOM-CIDOC's 'URIs and Linked Open Data' proposal for museum objects (http://www.cidoc-crm.org/URIs_and_Linked_Open_Data.html), opened for comment on the Crm-sig list in thread t0552 ('Call for Comments', starting 2011-03-21). The main objection, raised first by Maximilian Schich, was to paragraph 10c/11 of the draft, which implied a 'best institution for preserving a particular object's identifier' and let a designated aggregator take a leading role in minting/aggregating URIs for a set of objects. Schich argued this set up 'an artificial hierarchy of authority of who may issue the best identifier,' that in reality there is often no single best-placed institution, and that secondary/non-museum entities (scholars, auction houses like Artprice, online encyclopedias, PhD theses, etc.) should also be encouraged to mint identifiers as a fallback when museums don't, since competition among identifier-producers is part of normal scholarly practice; Vladimir Ivanov agreed with this objection, and Detlev Balzer separately worried that self-appointed 'leading national or community' aggregators would take on prestigious duties they couldn't sustain. Martin Doerr (the recommendation's author) responded on several fronts: he first pushed back that the recommendation's scope was strictly museum objects, not the art trade or cultural objects in general, and asked commenters to stay focused on what was actually proposed. On the substance, he argued that the recommendation already constrains aggregators via conditions in paragraph 11 (an aggregator role only applies if a curating institution takes no action, must never override a curating institution's own URIs, must publish a mapping between its URIs and any URIs the museum later issues, and must have a documented business relationship with the museum) -- and that examples given by objectors as 'good' aggregators (e.g. papyri.info/HGV, kulturarvsdata.se) actually fit and satisfy this leading-role model rather than contradicting it. He also gave a complexity/co-reference argument (citing Meghini, Doerr & Spyratos 2009) that reconciling an unconstrained web of competing identifiers grows exponentially hard, so keeping co-reference clusters star-shaped around a small number of authoritative URIs (ideally the museum's, with a controlled aggregator as fallback) keeps the problem tractable -- 'the more [identifiers], the worse.' He clarified the 'aggregators we fear are those that do not intend to curate their aggregations with scholarly care,' implying the recommendation is not against aggregation per se but against uncurated, uncontrolled minting.
notes: Thread t0552 ('Call for Comments', 2011) contained the full exchange: Martin Doerr posted the draft link, Maximilian Schich raised the authority/hierarchy objection (with Vladimir Ivanov concurring), and Martin Doerr replied in three follow-up messages defending the aggregator conditions already in paragraph 11 and the star-shaped co-reference complexity argument. A single hybrid search surfaced the thread directly; no further queries were needed.
